  data=list(y=NA, link=1)
for the prediction stack, and add
  link=inla.stack.data(stack)$link
to the control.predictor parameter list in the inla() call, I believe.

Finn

Hi,
I haven't followed the entire thread, but I think you should add n.group=k to all the inla.spde.make.A() calls so that they are setup to connect to the whole k-step spde model; otherwise the A-matrix for the observations will think there are at most 7 timesteps in the model, since it doesn't magically know that you actually want to build a model that extends beyond that, to k=8.

Predictions are setup exactly as ordinary observations, except that all the response values are set to NA, so that seems to be ok in your code now.

Finn

Ah, I missed that you have two likelihoods. You should set link=1 for stk.z and link=2 for stk.y (but I think they both have the same link, so it won't actually make a difference in this case).

> Do I make a prediction stack for z and y separately?

Yes, that would be easiest. For z-prediction, just include the covariates etc that make sense for z, and for y-prediction, just include the ones that make sense for y. The stack functions will join the stacks together as needed by adding NA vectors for "missing" effects. (NA in an effect vector means "no effect")

> Also, one last question just for clarification. Should the dataset for training have values in the last time step? Or do those need to be NAed out? I have 8 weeks of data. I am trying to predict the 8th week.

When you say "data", do you mean just covariate, or also response variables?
The way to think about these models is that they exist wether you observe the responses or not. So build the model to include any time steps that need to exist to make a coherent universe.

> Does INLA know based off of n.group=8 not to include the last week in the model training?

If you only have non-NA response variables for time steps 2 through 7, there is nothing to "train" for time step 8. The NA response "values" in the prediction stacks mean "these were not observed".

>     OK, but I fit the models jointly right, thus a "joint" model? In the precipitation example in the spde tutorial they fit the models separately then jointly. I am not looking for separately predictions of z and y, but rather 1 overall prediction based on the z and y likelihoods.

Well, the predictions are not on the data level, but rather on the linear model level, but apart from that, yes, the modeling and estimation is done jointly. However, the predictions are made for _something_, and if I understand correctly that would be for your GLM predictor models, of which there is one for z and one for y. Or I'm misunderstanding what you are trying to predict. You may need to spell out the actual mathematics of what your model is; R code only goes so far, and if it doesn't already describe what you want, then there is no way to figure it out without a proper model definition.

> So for the 1 prediction stack and 1 joint model how do I include the different inla.spde.make.index from z and y? That is where I am getting the name mismatch error. This is highlighted in the red part of my previous included code.

Please provide the exact error message.

Can you write down the two separate formula definitions you would have used if you were modeling z and y separately, as well as the joint model formula? The terms in those first 2 subformulas should be what you need to put in the respective stacks.
The joint model formula is just the union of those two formulas. This means that any effects that should be in both submodels must use the same names, and any effect that only should occur in one of the submodels must use a name that does not occur in the other submodel.  Each substack should then only include names used  corresponding subformula.

>      By data I mean both covariate values and response variables. I have values for all 8 weeks.

As I said, the mathematical model exists independently of any response variables. Prediction just means "for these values of the covariates (including spatial locations etc), what would I expect the observances to be?".

> Ideally this would eventually be an operational model where I would not have response variables or covariate models. As I am doing hindcast prediction right now, I have the data for the "next" week.

You can't do prediction (in time) without a model. In particular, if your model includes covariates, you must have them for the time/locations you want to do a prediction. If not, you should also have to build a prediction model for the covariates themselves.
(As I said, I haven't followed the entire thread, so I may be missing something obvious)

Finn

if you use a  mean=list() it must be named. [the question is if inla()

inla(y~1+a+b, control.fixed = list(mean = list(a=-1111)),

I am a newcomer to INLA (which I'm grateful to have discovered exists!), and am attempting to use it to model some biological time series data. There are S different subjects, from each of whom we have one time series (which, incidentally, occur at different and irregular time points). I would also be satisfied with other means of assessing out-of-sample performance at the group/subject/replicate level. (I know that the CPO/PIT values give insight into leave-one-observation-out performance, but it seems that this doesn't generalize to the group level?)

Does anyone have any advice on whether and how this might be possible? I apologize in advance if this question is based on misguided premises, or if the answer is somehow obvious (or both!)

Many thanks,
Jon

sigma2eps_marg = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/x, mod$marginals.hyperpar$"Precision for the Gaussian observations")

sigma2eps_m2 = inla.emarginal(function(x) x^2, sigma2eps_marg)

sigma2eps_stdev = sqrt(sigma2eps_m2 - sigma2eps_m1^2)

sigma2eps_quantiles = inla.qmarginal(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), sigma2eps_marg)

print(c(mean=sigma2eps_m1, sd=sigma2eps_stdev , "0.025quant" = sigma2eps_quantiles[1], "0.975quant" = sigma2eps_quantiles[3]))

Hi Elias,

When I follow the provided code I get this error when running inla: Any ideas? Can you explain what the difference between the three indexes are?  ix1, ix2, and iu?

Error in inla(form, family = c("binomial", "gamma"), data = inla.stack.data(jdat),  :
  Model component 'f(j, ...)' have only NA values in 'j'. In this case, either argument 'n' or 'values' must be spesified.

Here is my code:
library(sp)  # classes for spatial data

###########

FL_data1<-read.csv("FL_data22.csv",header=TRUE)
FL_data1<-FL_data1[,2:9] #correct data file removes leading columns

## define coordinates
FL_data4<-FL_data1[which(FL_data1$LONG<1462.861),]
FL_data5<-FL_data4[which(FL_data4$LONG>1451.527),]

FL_data6<-FL_data5[which(FL_data5$LAT<599.311),]
FL_data7<-FL_data6[which(FL_data6$LAT>584.225),]

rm(FL_data4)
rm(FL_data5)
rm(FL_data6)
coords<-FL_data7[1:695,4:5]

FL_data8<-FL_data7[which(FL_data7$time>14),]
FL_data8<-FL_data8[1:4865,]

#set up two datasets for Binomial/Gamma Hurdel model
z<-(FL_data8$Cyano>10232.93)+0
y<-ifelse(FL_data8$Cyano<10232.93,NA,1)*FL_data8$Cyano

###########################
###########################
mean_covariates2 = apply(FL_data8[,6:7],2,mean)
sd_covariates2 = apply(FL_data8[,6:7],2,sd)

FL_data8[,6:7] =
  scale(FL_data8[,6:7],
        mean_covariates2, sd_covariates2)

########### SET UP INLA...
loc<-cbind(coords$LONG,coords$LAT) #Stores the lat/long of each observation site

##### MAKE MESH
bnd<-inla.nonconvex.hull(loc,convex=1,resolution=(25)) #Makes a nonconvex hull around the points rather than the spatial extent of Florida
mesh=inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bnd,cutoff=.51,max.edge=c(1,8))
mesh$n

n_stations <- length(coords$LAT)
n_data <- length(FL_data8$Station.ID)
n_days <- as.integer(n_data/n_stations)
FL_data8$time = rep(1:n_days,each = n_stations)
i_day = 8

#Setting priors on the SPDE for variance and range
A <-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=as.matrix(coords[,1:2]))
sigma0 = 1
size = min(c(diff(range(mesh$loc[, 1])), diff(range(mesh$loc[, 2]))))
range0 = size / 5
kappa0 = sqrt(8) / range0
tau0 = 1 / (sqrt(4 * pi) * kappa0 * sigma0)
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh,alpha=2,
                         B.tau = cbind(log(tau0), -1, +1),
                         B.kappa = cbind(log(kappa0), 0, -1),
                         theta.prior.mean = c(0, 0),
                         theta.prior.prec = c(0.1, 1) )

#####
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(
  mesh=mesh,
  loc=
    as.matrix(coords[FL_data8$Station.ID,
                          c("LONG","LAT")]),
  group=FL_data8$time,
 n.group=n_days
)

#### make  index
ix1 <- inla.spde.make.index('i', spde$n.spde, n.group=n_days)
ix2 <- inla.spde.make.index('ic', spde$n.spde, n.group=n_days)
iu <- inla.spde.make.index('j', spde$n.spde, n.group=n_days)
#####
#######################EXAMPLE TO TRY with time component (ar1) and predictor (ATEMP, PRECIP) ############################

stk.z <- inla.stack(tag='est.z',
                    data=list(y=cbind(z, NA), link=1),

                    A=list(A.est, 1),
                    effects=list(
                      ix1,
                      data.frame(z.b0=1,Temp.z=FL_data8$Atemp,Prec.z=FL_data8$Precip)))

stk.y <- inla.stack(tag='est.y',
                    data=list(y=cbind(NA, y),

                              link=2),
                    A=list(A.est, 1),
                    effects=list(
                      c(ix2, iu),
                      data.frame(y.b0=1,Temp.y=FL_data8$Atemp,Prec.y=FL_data8$Precip)))

jdat <- inla.stack(stk.z, stk.y)#, pred.z,pred.y)

## set up model
form <- y ~ 0 + z.b0 +  y.b0 + Temp.z + Prec.z + Temp.y+Prec.y+
  f(i, model=spde, ##'generic0', Cmatrix=spde$param.inla$M2,
    group=i.group, control.group=list(model='ar1')) +
  f(ic, copy='i', group=ic.group, fixed=FALSE) +
  f(j, model=spde, group=j.group, control.group=list(model='ar1'))

### run INLA model
res <- inla(form, family=c('binomial', 'gamma'),
            data=inla.stack.data(jdat),
            verbose=TRUE,
            control.inla=list(strategy='gaussian'),
            control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(jdat),
                                   compute=TRUE,
                                   link=inla.stack.data(jdat)$link))

print(summary(res))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
  I'm fitting a geostatistical model to some count data which has an excess number of zeros. I wish to use covariates to explain both the count data itself, and the probability that the count is zero. I have used both the advanced example found in the zeroinflated r-inla document here https://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf plus the SPDE tutorial example for rainfall data found here http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/tutorials/spde/spde-tutorial.pdf to fit my model, where I use family=c("binomial","zeroinflatednbinomial1").

I am a little confused as to how to make predictions that both combine the binomial and negative binomial elements. For example, using the SPDE tutorial example and the model in section 6.3

res.zy <- inla(y ~ 0 + z.b0 + y.b0 + f(i.z, model=spde) + f(i.y, copy='i.z', fixed=FALSE), family=c('binomial', 'gamma'), data=inla.stack.data(stk.zy), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.zy), compute=TRUE))

and

then res.zy$summary.fitted.values[iy,1] will give me the posterior mean for the counts, but I think assumes the counts come from a gamma distribution, without taking into account the zero-inflated part.

Are my assumptions correct? And if so, how would I get the fitted counts for the model that incorporate the probability that the counts are zero?

Thanks,
  Shell

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
It is hard to understand your problem without seeing the data, but it looks like you are fitting a gamma hurdle model, rather than one of the likelihoods for zero inflated data. So your intent seems to be to have a bernoulli variate for the 0/1 and a gamma (for a continuous response, rather than discrete counts) for the samples where y>0?
Then the expectation for y_i given the covariates should be the product of the expectations for the bernoulli and gamma processes (e.g. see http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/81457/what-is-the-difference-between-zero-inflated-and-hurdle-distributions-models/81532#81532).
I am not sure of the best way to implement this production as a prediction from R-INLA, so hopefully someoen else can help you there.
Cheers,
Chris

Hi,
I've just written a prototype "shiny" tool to help answer this very question!
It will soon be part of the package, but I'll put up a temporary link tomorrow.
Brief rules of thumb:
1) for alpha=2 (the default spde models), most parameter estimation bias is gone if max.edge is smaller than a 10th of the correlation range. In practice, one can often let max.edge be a bit larger than that. (Bolin&Lindgren 2015 or 2016 says more about this; I'll get the precise reference...)
2) the domain extension to move he boundary effects away from the domain of interest needs to be about the size of the correlation length.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Haakon,

Sorry about the delayed reply. My code is messy and spread across several files/classes, so I'll describe the approach and please let me know if you'd like to see any actual code and I'll try to put together a more readable standalone example. The thing I have tried to compute (hopefully correctly - I welcome any comments/criticisms!) is the log pointwise predictive density as described in section 2.3 of this paper <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf> by Vehtari and Gelman.

Here's the gist of what I'm doing. Suppose I have 50 subjects (each with many observations) in my data.frame (df) and will hold out 10 for each fold (5-fold CV). For the first fold, I then make a copy (y1) of my response variable with all values set to NA for all observations for the 10 test subjects in fold 1. Now I call INLA using y1 as the response, and then pass the fitted model to inla.posterior.sample to get 1000 samples from the joint hyperparameter-and-latent posterior. Suppose I have N total test observations from my 10 test subjects. I can pull out the N simulated values of the linear predictor for my 10 test subjects from each draw and put them all into a 1000xN matrix -- call it y1_sim (since I am using identity link, these are on the y scale). For each posterior draw we also have a corresponding precision, so I put these into a 1000-vector (tau_sim). Finally, let y1_true be the N-vector of true observations in the test fold.

Then (I think!) the estimated log predictive density (aka log likelihood) for the fold should result from the final sum below:

residuals <- sweep(y_sim, 2, y_true) #subtract true values from each row of y_sim
log_dens <- dnorm(residuals, sd=sqrt(1/tau_sim), log=TRUE) #log likelihood of the residual of each draw
lpd <- apply(log_dens, 2, function (col) {log_sum_exp(col) - log(length(col))}) #take mean across draws (rows) for each point, giving pointwise likelihoods; using log_sum_exp in case of underflow
sum(ldp) # joint likelihood for this test set (?)

Of course all of these depends on e.g. my having interpreted the output of e.g. inla.posterior.sample correctly. I'm grateful for any pointers if I'm on the wrong track here!

Cheers,
Jonathan

there isn't any paper on this (I just added it because we needed it at
some point).  the documentation says what happens

    The hyperparameters are sampled from the configurations used to do
     the numerical integration, hence if you want a higher resolution,
     you need to to change the ‘int.stratey’ variable and friends. The
     latent field is sampled from the Gaussian approximation
     conditioned on the hyperparameters, but with a correction for the
     mean (default).

although its to short to know really what is going on, maybe.

as said, it uses the integration points to sample the hyperparameters,
so that is why you see only a finite number of configurations. for each
hyperparameter is sample the latent from the Gaussian approximation. In
most cases, ther is available a correction for the mean (like its
computed with the simplified.laplace or the laplace), then the mean of
this Gaussian is corrected, but the precision matrix is not.

its possible to correct also for skewness, but no-one has got around to
do this as its potentially quite timeconsuming, well, maybe not.

hope this helps!

PS: if someone wants to write this up properly and maybe do a
comparison, please let us know!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Tools to flag when INLA is inaccurate?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Tools to flag when INLA is inaccurate?
messages.body_plain:
The simplest thing to do would be to think like a numericist:
Increase the quality of the approximations, e.g.
- integration strategy
- laplace approx strategy
- numerical optimisation
- hessian computation

and check that the result is stable and "looks converging".

But there are no automated tools for this yet. What I do is just look at the verbose output and see that the optimisation looks reasonable, since this is the only part I know that there can be bad behaviour.

For many of the interesting problems we solve, you do not have time for an "MCMC that has run for a very very long time".

The laplace approximation itself is usually very good already for "n=2" in my experience. With the exception that I am not sure about its quality when you have extremely many zeroes in count data.

Kind regards,
Haakon

>From your code, I understand that you compute for each sample (s)
\pi(y_i | predictor_{i,s}, tau_s),

and integrate over the posterior (by averaging over the posterior samples).

Also, this way of computing the joint is a very good idea.

The only limitation I see is for "strange data" (data that is "surprising" to the model, the test data where your fit is bad). Here, your sample size may be very small. E.g. if most of the predictive probability comes from, say, 3 samples, and the rest is negligible, then your ESS (effective sample size) is not 1000, but closer to 3. And in this case, the estimated density may be inaccurate.

             data=data1, control.family=list(link='logit'),

> Is it possible to control the mesh size by a user specified function in inla.mesh.2d()? Say, a function describing the distance from the boundary when the sampling points are designed to be dense near the boundary but sparse within.

inla.mesh.create() supports a version of this via the quality.spec parameter, but not inla.mesh.2d().
quality.spec allows the user to specify individual max.edge values for each input point, that are then interpolated to other locations as needed.
It's a bit fiddly to get the desired effect from this, so a perhaps easier alternative is to specify a two-stage mesh build in inla.mesh.2d() where the interior of the domain is the second stage. This is done by having the first boundary include a "some distance from the boundary of the domain" boundary.

Finn

Hello,

I am trying to do model development with count data, however all models with a spatial component have CPO failures on the majority of the data.

The spatial data I am using is county-level reported rape counts for about 2600 US counties. I initially assumed the data would be overdispersed, however I conducted an initial Vuong's test using other R packages to estimate poisson and zero-inflated poisson models (with no spatial component) and the poisson performed better. I should mention that the crime reports are averaged for each county across 5 years and then rounded up to the nearest unit and only about 230 of the counties have 0 crime, which might explain why the zero-inflated poisson is not necessary.

If I estimate an intercept only model with no spatial component, there are no CPO failures:

form.null <- avg_rape_rounded ~ 1

model.null <- inla(form.null, family='poisson',
                   data=df, offset=log(log_10k_pop_offset),
                   control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo=TRUE),
                   control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE))

sum(model.null$cpo$failure) == 0

However, when I add the spatial component, there are a lot of CPO failures:

form.null.spatial <- as.formula(paste0('avg_rape_rounded ~ 1 + f(idx, model="bym", graph=county_graph)'))

model.null.spatial <- inla(form.null.spatial, family = 'poisson',
                         data=spdf@data,
                         control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo=TRUE),
                         control.predictor=list(link=1, compute=TRUE))

sum(model.null.spatial$cpo$failure) == 2678.776

I tried re-computing the CPOs, but this never converged:

improved.result <- inla.cpo(model.null.spatial, verbose=T)

Finally, I tried running bym2 and besag, and bym with the zeroinflatedpoisson1 family. This later setting reduced the CPO failure to 2506.099.

I found this old thread: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/gu9aqg3SIUc, which suggested changing the hyperparameter priors for a besag model that was having the same issue. However, I still received the same error.

I have attached my a SpatialPolygonDataFrame object with an id variable (idx), the dv, and an offset, as well as code for producing the two models above. I am giving a presentation on these analyses this week, so it would be very, very appreciated if anyone could offer some insight about why I am getting CPO failure.

Also, as you can probably guess, I am new to R-INLA and spatial analysis. I have read as widely as possible, but it is still all rather foreign. I understand what CPO represents, and I would just like to confirm that CPO failures across the board, like I am seeing, mean that a model is unreliable. I guess what is confusing me is that the other model fit indices seem reasonable, as do the parameter estimates. Any higher-level thoughts on this would also be really helpful.

Thank you in advance.

Best,
Joe

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] CPO failure on majority of data
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] CPO failure on majority of data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am used to having many nonzero $cpo$failure for count data. Having many failures does not mean that a model is bad.

# INLA cpo failures
This failure means that the assumptions needed to approximate the hold-out point using the inla.result object are not appropriate. (Any inference algorithm, MCMC or INLA, only explores parts of the posterior. If the posterior changes too much when removing a datapoint, the posterior must be explored more; the model must be re-run.)

I take this to mean that there is a slight conflict between model and the failure points. This is not actually a computational problem, this is just how it is with your model and your data. Running "inla.cpo" will re-run the model possibly several thousand times, and may take almost forever.

Personally, I believe that "many cpo failures" implies that the only way to perform good predictive measures of fit is to rerun the model several times (on training/testing sets). This is because any approximative predictive measure will be dependent on this same faulty representation of the "predictive model".

In my experience, adding more random effects often reduce the "sum(model.null$cpo$failure)". But this does not mean that you have a better model.

# Measures of fit (without prediction)
You can compare the fit to the observations directly, to see that your model is not completely wrong, in the usual way.

I attached a script with an example of how to do this. Please do not take this to mean "the model is good", only to mean that the model is "not horrible" :)

# Zero inflation
Zero-inflation type 0 (one of the standard ones) are equivalent to removing the zeroes from your dataset. This is usually not what you want. If a zero means that "there are few incidents there" then you do not want this zero inflation. If a zero means "I did not measure anything here" then you definitely want this type of zero inflation.

Zero inflated type 1: Some of my zeroes are because I measured and there was nothing. A random (unstructured) process turned many of the other observations into zeroes also. Again, this model may also be worse than the "poisson" model.

I hope this "high-level" was helpful. Let me know if any part was confusing.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

Depending on what you want, you could:

1. Use the gaussian prior
2. Plot prior and posterior of fixed effect
3. Ensure that the prior you want (e.g. uniform) and the prior that you used (gaussian) are the same "in that plot"

What the prior is away from the likelihood/posterior is not that important, after all. So as long as they behave nearly identically where your likelihood/posterior is, you may be able to sell the Gaussian prior as a computational trick.

Haakon

messages.subject: Multiplicative measurement error
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to apply the SPDE model to fit some spatial data (x,y;h). Usually we assume h has multiplicative measurement error to some degree, saying 10%, i.e. h = h0+h0*e, where h0 is the true underlying spatial process and the measure error ratio e is around 10%. If I want to model the true spatial process h0 with the SPDE approach, what can I do with R-INLA? A simple approach I can come up with is to take log transformation, log(h) = log(h0)+log(1+e). In this way I can use the ordinary Gaussian family with assumptions on log(1+e) as additive error. But I am worried about two issues here: (1) my h lies in the real number range so that sometimes log(h) is not well defined; (2) I need to assume log(h0) to be the Gaussian process here, but I want h0 to be the Gaussian process. Could anyone help me with this problem? Thanks!

Kind regards,
Michael

On possibility is to linearise the model and iterate the inla estimations;
eta = x + x*e
would turn into
eta = -x0*e0 + (1+e0)*x + x0*e
where x0 and e0 are the posterior medians for x and e from the previous iteration.
This turns the problem into a sequence of problems that can be implemented in R-INLA.

We're working on methods for similar problems in a current project, but it's not ready to share yet.

messages.body_plain:
The needed parameter is weights= rather than scale=, but the real issue is inla only allows you to do that for already known weights (the predictor must be linear in all the latent variables). So the iteration/linearisation idea is based on the idea of using an estimate x0 of x as weight instead of x itself. The new estimate x is then the x0 needed for the next iteration.  The full linearisation I indicated can perhaps be replaced by only using weights=x0 in the formula you wrote, and ignore the rest of the full linearisation equation, but I can't guarantee the stability of that without doing maths...  But if it converges it's at least an easier solution.

There may be some other tricks for achieving the same thing.

Finn
